## What does SPI measure?

The surveillance performance index (SPI) compares a district's current reporting with its earlier reporting, then compares that change with the national pattern. It uses non-polio acute flaccid paralysis (NPAFP) case counts and the population under 15.

It is calculated in three steps:

1. Estimate the expected number of NPAFP cases from the district's own earlier reporting and its current under-15 population.
2. Divide the reported cases by the expected cases. This is the district's observed-to-expected (O/E) ratio.
3. Divide the district's ratio by the national ratio for the same year.

An SPI of 1 means the district's ratio equals the national ratio. An SPI of 0.6 means the district's ratio is 60% of the national ratio. Check both ratios to see whether reporting fell below earlier levels: an SPI below 1 can also occur when reporting increased nationally but increased less in the district.

## How is it different from the NPAFP rate?

The conventional NPAFP rate is the number of reported cases per 100,000 children under 15 per year. It is compared with a fixed target, such as 3, regardless of the district's earlier reporting.

SPI compares each district with its own history and the national ratio. A district can report fewer cases than expected from earlier years and still meet the NPAFP target. SPI can identify this decline if it is larger than the national decline. A district that has reported few cases for years can have an SPI near 1 while staying below the NPAFP target.

The two measures answer different questions, so read them together. [Interpreting SPI](spi-interpretation.html) works through examples, and `spi_compare_npafp()` places each district-year in one of the four combinations.

## Which SPI should I use?

The package calculates expected counts in two ways. Both use earlier reporting, and the resulting SPI values have the same interpretation.

| | Simple SPI | Model-based SPI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Function | `spi_simple()` | `spi_index()` |
| Expected count from | The district's own earlier rate | A spatial and temporal model |
| District reporting history | Yes | Yes |
| Statistical model | No | Yes |
| INLA | No | Yes |
| Boundary files | No | Yes, or a neighbour graph |
| Input counts | Annual | Monthly |
| Uncertainty intervals | No | Yes |
| Short or sparse history | SPI unavailable without an earlier case | More stable estimates |
| Monthly estimates | No | Yes |
| Comparison with the NPAFP target | Yes | Yes |
| STEPS field guide | Yes; default SPI cutoff of 0.5 | Yes; uses the credible interval |

Start with the simple SPI for annual results. You can check each value by hand using case counts, population and the national ratio.

Use the model-based SPI when you need uncertainty intervals, monthly estimates, or more stable expected counts for districts with little reporting history.

## A first example

The bundled `synth_surveillance` data cover 236 districts in the fictional country Harad, from 2015 to 2024. The case counts are monthly, so first add them up by year:


``` r
library(spi)

annual <- synth_surveillance$cases |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(format(month, "%Y"))) |>
  dplyr::summarise(count = sum(count), .by = c(adm2_guid, year))
```

Then calculate the simple SPI, naming the columns that hold the district ID, the case count and the under-15 population:


``` r
spi_results <- spi_simple(
  data = annual,
  population = synth_surveillance$population,
  id_col = "adm2_guid",
  count_col = "count",
  pop_col = "pop_u15",
  verbose = FALSE
)

spi_results
```

`tibble::as_tibble(spi_results)` gives one row per district and year with the observed and expected counts, both ratios and the SPI.

Compare the SPI with the NPAFP target:


``` r
comparison <- spi_compare_npafp(spi_results, npafp_target = 3, verbose = FALSE)

comparison$metrics |>
  dplyr::select(n, n_neither, n_spi_only, n_npafp_only, n_both)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>       n n_neither n_spi_only n_npafp_only n_both
#>   <int>     <int>      <int>        <int>  <int>
#> 1  1644       678        742           42    182
```

`n_spi_only` counts district-years that met the NPAFP target but had an SPI below 1. Their observed-to-expected ratio was below the national ratio, even though they met the reporting target.

- [Preparing data for SPI](spi-data-preparation.html) shows how to build the input tables.
- [Using SPI with POLIS data](spi-polis.html) starts from the POLIS AFP line list.
- [Interpreting SPI](spi-interpretation.html) explains what the results mean and what they do not.
- [How SPI works](spi-methods.html) explains both calculations and their limitations.

For the simple SPI, [Calculating the simple SPI](spi-simple.html) works through three districts by hand and repeats the calculation in R.

For the model-based SPI, [Calculating the model-based SPI](spi-model.html) fits the model, [Model options and sensitivity](spi-model-options.html) covers the model choices, and [Using SPI for district review](spi-field-guide.html) runs the STEPS field guide.
